meta: Jørgen Wichfeld in a white wig and grey coat: Isak Wacklin's 1749 portrait, bought by the Finnish National Gallery in 2007.
about: A man in a white wig, a grey coat over a yellow waistcoat and lace at neck and cuffs poses before a red drape in this oil portrait of Jørgen Wichfeld. Isak Wacklin painted it in 1749. The picture stood at Engestofte Manor in Denmark until it was sold at Christie's in London on 31 October 2007 for 2,500 pounds. The Finnish National Gallery bought it that December.

meta: An imagined Rhine landscape with a hilltop town and a ferry: Kasparus Karsen's painting of 1840, signed K. Karsten.
about: The Rijksmuseum calls this an imagined river landscape in the region of the Rhine. On the right bank a town climbs a hill, topped by a castle and a cathedral with twin towers. A ferry carries people across the water in the foreground. On a cobbled quay a woman and child walk past low brick houses. The signature at the bottom centre reads K. Karsten.

meta: Prince Frederick Henry and Count Ernst Casimir above the camp at 's-Hertogenbosch: Pauwels van Hillegaert's painting of the 1629 siege.
about: Prince Frederick Henry sits on his horse on a hill and points his commander's staff at the besieged city of 's-Hertogenbosch. Count Ernst Casimir waits at the right on a grey horse. Below them lie the tents of the besieging armies, and in the distance burning fortifications mark the city's outline. Pauwels van Hillegaert painted the siege of 1629. An inventory made when it moved from The Hague to Het Loo in 1763 described it as showing Princes Maurits and Frederick Henry on horseback. It was first recorded in the museum in 1800.

meta: Two exiles on a pair of screens: Unkoku Togan's early 1600s painting of the poets Su Shi and Pan Lang.
about: Two men sent into exile appear on this pair of screens, one on each. In the left screen the official Pan Lang rides his donkey backward so that he can look once more at Mount Hua as he returns from banishment. In the right screen the poet Su Shi sets off into exile. Pan had written a careless verse about one of the king's horses, and Su Shi's comments on economic reforms were read as criticism of the emperor. Unkoku Togan founded the Unkoku school and served the Mori family.

meta: Two riders wait at a gate held open by a woman: Walter Ufer's 1920 painting of an everyday moment among New Mexico's Pueblo people.
about: Two riders on brown horses wait beside a white picket fence under a leafy tree while a woman in a dark hooded shawl and blue dress holds the gate open. Walter Ufer painted the scene in 1920. The Smithsonian American Art Museum calls it an everyday yet deeply poetic moment among New Mexico's Pueblo people. Ufer was a German immigrant. The museum says his socialist family gave him a strong sympathy for ordinary people.

meta: A reader at a pavilion among pines: Wang Meng's album leaf, with his own inscription in seal script.
about: Tall twisted pines rise beside a thatched pavilion where a robed figure sits at a small table. Rugged mountains and a wooden footbridge over a stream surround him. Wang Meng wrote the inscription on the right in classical seal script and put his signature and seal on the left. He was a grandson of Zhao Mengfu through his mother and spent most of his life in retirement. In the 1360s he withdrew into the mountains north of Hangzhou, and early in the Ming dynasty he was caught up in a purge and died in prison.
credit_line: Bequest of Mrs. A. Dean Perry

meta: King Liuva I of the Visigoths in a white tunic and crimson mantle: Antonio Gisbert's portrait of 1855.
about: King Liuva I stands in profile with his face turned toward the viewer, in a white tunic and crimson mantle, one hand on a long scepter. He reigned from 567 to 572 and had been duke of Septimania before he was proclaimed king in Narbonne. To avoid needless conflict he made his brother, his successor, a partner on the throne. The brother ruled Hispania while Liuva kept Gaul. The museum's note says this broke with earlier Gothic kings, who tried to secure their own hold on power. Antonio Gisbert painted him in 1855.

meta: Joseph, Mary and a shepherd admire the Christ Child: Battista Dossi's Holy Family of the early 1520s, once given to his brother Dosso.
about: Joseph and Mary lean in to admire the Christ Child while a shepherd in a blue cloak looks on, resting on his staff. Silvery-blue moonlight touches a thickly wooded landscape. The Cleveland Museum of Art sees a second style here, which Battista Dossi began after a visit to Rome where he studied Raphael closely. It shows in the flexible pose of Christ, the small hands and the high foreheads. The painting was first given to his brother Dosso. Both worked as court painters to Duke Alfonso I of Ferrara. The museum bought it in 1949 from Giuseppe Cellini of Rome.
credit_line: Delia E. Holden and L. E. Holden Funds

meta: Emperor Ming Huang and Yang Guifei in a palace garden: a Japanese Kano school screen of about 1700.
about: Flowers bloom everywhere as the emperor and Yang Guifei meet in a palace garden. On the left a blossoming tree stands over a group of court women, and on the right the emperor sits on a terrace with red railings, attended by officials. The story comes from the Song of Everlasting Sorrow, a poem by Bo Juyi about Emperor Ming Huang, whose love for his concubine threw his empire into disorder. Her death followed in the uprising of 756. The artist is unknown. The museum sees the style of the Kano school.

meta: Ulysses S. Grant in a trench at Vicksburg: Ole Peter Hansen Balling's portrait of 1861.
about: Ulysses S. Grant stands in a trench during the siege of Vicksburg in 1863, with a map on the table beside him showing the Mississippi River. He is bearded and wears a slouch hat and dark uniform, with binoculars and a cigar at his side. The Norwegian-born painter Ole Peter Hansen Balling had briefly served as a Union soldier at the start of the Civil War and went back to painting after he was wounded. The museum adds that Grant won at Fort Donelson in 1862 and that Lincoln made him lieutenant general in 1864.

meta: Snow on the slope of Arashiyama: Shiokawa Bunrin's hanging scroll, which uses bare silk for the snow.
about: A steep slope of Arashiyama fills the scroll, a mountain on the bank of the Oi River that people from Kyoto liked to visit. Snow-laden pines rise beside misty peaks. The painter left the silk unpainted to stand for white snow. Age and exposure have darkened the silk, so the effect was stronger at first. The museum says the realism comes partly from Shiokawa Bunrin's knowledge of European painting techniques, which he combined with Japanese materials and brush methods.

meta: Episodes from the life of Saint John the Baptist on one panel: Bartolomeo di Giovanni's tempera painting of 1490 to 1495.
about: Several episodes from the life of Saint John the Baptist share one panel, set inside a classical building with a coffered ceiling and a tiled floor. On the left, figures stand in a rural landscape. The panel may have belonged to a set of decorations made for Francesco Pitti in Florence, because the arms on a related panel in Dublin point to him. Luigi Grassi sold it to the Chicago collector Martin A. Ryerson in 1924. Ryerson's widow inherited it, and it came to the Art Institute by bequest in 1937.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: The Elizabethan entrance hall of East Sutton Place in Kent: a watercolour by Charles James Richardson, 1840.
about: East Sutton Place in Kent, parts of which go back to the time of Henry VIII, was the family seat of Sir Edmund Filmer, a baronet and member of Parliament. This watercolour shows its entrance hall with carved Elizabethan walls and ceiling. The square pattern of the marble floor echoes the ceiling. Chairs, suits of armour and Oriental ceramics probably stay close to the original Tudor scheme for the hall. Charles James Richardson drew it in 1840.

meta: Seasons from plum blossom to peonies: Kano Mitsunobu's screen of birds and flowers from the late 1500s.
about: Seasons run from right to left across this pair of screens, starting with a blossoming plum in early spring and ending with peonies in late autumn. At the centre three ducks swim between early summer irises and early autumn bellflowers. To the right, birds of prey go after a pheasant and an egret, while on the left a peacock and peahen seem to talk. The museum reads the hawks as a sign of military strength and the peafowl as a sign of cultural prestige. Kano Mitsunobu painted them in the late 1500s.

meta: Three Chinese-taste torcheres with dolphins, a dragon and a flute player: plate 13 of Thomas Johnson's One Hundred and Fifty New Designs.
about: Three torcheres in the Chinese taste stand side by side on one sheet. The right one is scrollwork supporting two dolphins whose tails intertwine. The centre one is heavy rocaille with a dog where the legs cross and a dragon on top. The left one is rocaille with tree branches and a flute player. Names and date are engraved below. The sheet is plate 13 of One Hundred and Fifty New Designs.

meta: Bartholomeus Strobel's huge Feast of Herod with the Beheading of St John the Baptist, a banquet crowded with portraits of Thirty Years' War figures.
about: A banquet hall crowded with courtiers fills most of this canvas, which is about nine and a half metres wide. Herod Antipas feasts at the left while his daughter Salome produces the head of John the Baptist. The execution is small, at the right. Many faces are portraits of leading figures of the Thirty Years' War. One reading takes the picture as an appeal to the Christian world to save Silesia, the painter's doomed home. It has been dated anywhere from the 1630s to the early 1640s.
